newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Police out in force as few Albanians dare protest.
newsitem.headline: Police out in force as few Albanians dare protest.

text.p: Police were out in force on Sunday as a handful of Albanians gathered at rallies to demand the dismissal of the right-wing government and compensation for savings they lost in collapsed pyramid investment schemes.
Scores of uniformed and plain clothes police cordoned off roads leading to a soccer pitch in Tirana where a trade union rally had been due to take place.
Police officers were seen arguing with trade union boss Azem Hajdari, the student leader hailed as a hero six years ago for helping to topple the hardline communist regime.
Witnesses said they were trying to persuade him to leave the area because he had not received permission to hold the meeting.

Hajdari supporters had urged workers and students on Saturday to stage a peaceful meeting in Tirana to voice their disapproval at the way the Democratic Party government has handled the pyramid scheme financial scandal.
"All come at the rally, leave behind your party differences," the union said in an invitation in the independent Koha Jone newspaper.
But few people were seen near the soccer pitch, where police broke up a Hajdari-led gathering last week before it had time to begin.
Albanians have been clearly frightened by a wave of arrests, reported beatings and intimidation since last weekend's violent protests across the Balkan state.
Authorities have said at least 149 people were arrested during the week on charges of instigating violence and those convicted could face minimum sentences of 15 years.
One senior opposition Socialist was mysteriously beaten up in central Tirana on Wednesday by unknown assailants.
Hajdari, who co-founded the Democratic Party in 1990 and is a member of parliament, has not been threatened but he has said he could well be detained if troubles increased.
He still backs President Sali Berisha, but distanced himself from the ruling clique last year after warning against the lack of government action against dubious pyramid schemes.

While small cracks began appearing in the dominant Democratic Party, the opposition also called rallies in the Adriatic port of Durres, 40 km (25 miles) west of Tirana, and in the town of Lezhe further north.

In Durres, witnesses said up to 500 people, mainly old men, had made their way to the town soccer stadium. Uniformed and plain clothes police, in vans and on foot, were out in force but were keeping their distance.

One elderly man said there were three reasons why so few people had attended the rally. "Firstly, there were so many police outside the stadium, secondly because the Democrats here have warned people that if they demonstrate they will lose their state jobs, and thirdly, because of the arrests."
There were no immediate reports of events in Lezhe.

The poorly-attended rallies were in stark contrast to the wave of violence that swept the Balkan state last weekend when angry crowds got of control, torching government buildings and Democratic Party offices in towns in the south.
Thousands demonstrated in central Tirana last Sunday, hurling stones and clashing with riot police who broke up the protest by force.

Berisha has promised that people will receive some of the cash they invested in two failed pyramid schemes by next Wednesday. But it appeared most would be given bank certificates and have to wait months before seeing any of their cash. Others may get nothing back.
